summary: Defines how LDAP distinguished names are written as text strings, using UTF-8. It tries to give a clean form for common names while being able to represent any name. It replaces RFC 1779 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4514.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory name is a list of pieces, each saying something about the thing being named, such as its common name or its country. RFC 2253 gives the exact text format for that list, so that a name written by one program is read the same way by another, including names that contain commas, quotes or letters outside English.

subtitle: How a directory name is written as text, and read back again.

tldr.problem: The X.500 directory uses distinguished names as the keys to its entries and encodes them in ASN.1. LDAP carries them as plain text, so there has to be one agreed way to write a name as a string and read it back.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2253 gives an algorithm for converting a distinguished name into a string and a grammar for parsing that string back. It uses a short name for each attribute type where one is known, an equals sign, the value, a plus sign between the parts of a multi-valued name and a comma between names.
tldr.outcome: The rules cover escaping, so that a value can contain a comma, a quote or any character outside plain ASCII, and they accept the older LDAPv2 forms on input while refusing to produce them. The document was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4514.

facts.label: Short attribute type names
facts.value: CN, L, ST, O, OU, C, STREET, DC and UID

today: RFC 2253 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1779 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4514, and updated by RFC 3377.

sections.title: Background and Goals
sections.content:
The X.500 Directory uses distinguished names as the primary keys to its entries, and encodes them in ASN.1 in the X.500 directory protocols. In the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, a string representation of distinguished names is transferred instead. This specification defines that string format, and it is designed to give a clean representation of commonly used distinguished names while still being able to represent any distinguished name.

A common format matters because a distinguished name has to be represented unambiguously. The primary goal of the specification is ease of encoding and decoding. The secondary goal is names that are human readable. The RFC does not expect an LDAP client with a user interface to show these strings directly, but rather to translate them, for example by expressing attribute type names in the user's own language.

The document also carries the same warning as the rest of the LDAPv3 series. Until mandatory authentication mechanisms are standardised, clients and servers that make use of update functionality are unlikely to interoperate, or may interoperate only if authentication is reduced to an unacceptably weak level. Implementors are discouraged from deploying such clients and servers in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory entries are looked up by a name that is a list of facts about the entry, such as the country and the organisation. The list has to be written down in one agreed way, so that every program reading it gets the same answer.

sections.title: Turning a Distinguished Name into Text
sections.content:
In X.501 the ASN.1 structure of a distinguished name is a sequence of relative distinguished names, each of which is a set of attribute type and value pairs.

To convert that structure into a string, an empty sequence becomes the empty string. Otherwise the output is the string encoding of each relative distinguished name, starting with the last element of the sequence and moving backwards toward the first. The encodings of adjoining relative distinguished names are separated by a comma character, ASCII 44.

Each relative distinguished name becomes the string encodings of its attribute type and value pairs, in any order, and where the name has more than one pair the outputs of adjoining pairs are separated by a plus character, ASCII 43.

Each attribute type and value pair is written as the string representation of the type, an equals character, ASCII 61, and then the string representation of the value. If the type appears in the published table of attribute types associated with LDAP, the short name from that table is used. Otherwise the type is written as the dotted-decimal encoding of its object identifier. The table gives CN for commonName, L for localityName, ST for stateOrProvinceName, O for organizationName, OU for organizationalUnitName, C for countryName, STREET for streetAddress, DC for domainComponent and UID for userid.

The value itself is written in one of two ways. If the attribute value has no string representation defined for it, it is written as an octothorpe character, ASCII 35, followed by the hexadecimal representation of each byte of the BER encoding of the value. This form should be used when the attribute type is in the dotted-decimal form. Otherwise the value is converted to a UTF-8 string according to its syntax specification.

That UTF-8 string needs escaping if it has a space or a hash character at the beginning, a space character at the end, or one of the characters comma, plus, quotation mark, backslash, less-than, greater-than or semicolon. Implementations may escape other characters. A character on the list is prefixed with a backslash. Any other character to be escaped is replaced by a backslash and two hexadecimal digits that give the byte for that character.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is written from the end backwards, so the most specific piece comes first. Each piece is a short name, an equals sign and a value. A comma separates the pieces and a plus sign separates the parts of a piece that has more than one part.

sections.title: Parsing Text back into a Distinguished Name
sections.content:
The structure of the string is given as a BNF grammar based on the grammar in RFC 822. A distinguished name may be the empty string. A name is one or more name components separated by commas. A name component is one or more attribute type and value pairs separated by plus signs, and each pair is an attribute type, an equals sign and a value. The attribute type is either a name made of a letter followed by letters, digits or hyphens, or an object identifier written as numbers separated by dots.

The value is a string, which is either a run of ordinary characters and escape pairs, or a hash followed by a hex string, or, only from version 2, a quotation mark, a run of characters and a closing quotation mark. Inside the quoted value the comma, equals, plus, less-than, greater-than, hash and semicolon may all appear without escaping. A pair is a backslash followed by one of the special characters, a backslash, a quotation mark, or a pair of hexadecimal digits.

Server implementations that parse a DN string generated by an LDAPv2 client must also accept, and ignore, the variants given in the next section.
sections.plainLanguage: To read a name back, you split it on the commas, split each piece on the plus signs, and split each of those on the first equals sign. What is left is the type on one side and the value on the other, with any backslash escapes undone.

sections.title: Relationship with RFC 1779 and LDAPv2
sections.content:
The syntax in this document is more restrictive than the syntax in RFC 1779. Implementations that parse a string generated by an LDAPv2 client must accept the RFC 1779 syntax. Implementations must not, however, generate any of the RFC 1779 encodings that are not described in the conversion section.

Four older forms have to be accepted on input. A semicolon may be used instead of a comma to separate relative distinguished names, and whitespace may appear on either side of the comma or semicolon; the whitespace is ignored and the semicolon is replaced with a comma. An object identifier in the attribute type may be prefixed with the character string "oid." or "OID.". Spaces may appear between a name component and a comma, between an attribute type and value pair and a plus sign, between an attribute type and the equals sign, and between the equals sign and the value. And a value may be surrounded by quotation marks, which are not part of the value, inside which the comma, equals, plus, less-than, greater-than, hash and semicolon may all appear without escaping.
sections.plainLanguage: Older programs wrote names in a slightly looser way, using a semicolon instead of a comma, or putting spaces in odd places, or quoting the value. A reader has to understand those, but a writer must use the tidy form.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The notation is designed to be convenient for the common forms of name. A name with three relative distinguished names is written CN=Steve Kille,O=Isode Limited,C=GB.

An example with three relative distinguished names in which the first is multi-valued is written OU=Sales+CN=J. Smith,O=Widget Inc.,C=US.

An example showing how a comma inside an organisation name is quoted is written CN=L. Eagle,O=Sue\, Grabbit and Runn,C=GB. An example with a carriage return character in the value is written CN=Before\0DAfter,O=Test,C=GB.

An example in which a relative distinguished name was of an unrecognised type, so the value is the BER encoding of an OCTET STRING containing the two bytes 0x48 and 0x69, is written 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=#04024869,O=Test,C=GB.

The last example shows a surname value of five letters, including two that are not in plain ASCII. The Latin small letter C with a caron has the 10646 code U0000010D, is 0xC48D in UTF-8, and is written \C4\8D. The Latin small letter C with an acute has the code U00000107, is 0xC487 in UTF-8, and is written \C4\87. Together the five letters can be written in printable ASCII, which is useful for debugging, as SN=Lu\C4\8Di\C4\87.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a plain name, a name with two parts in one piece, a name with a comma in it, and a name with letters outside plain English. The last of those can also be written using only plain ASCII characters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Distinguished names typically consist of descriptive information about the entries they name, which can be people, organizations, devices or other real-world objects. That frequently includes the common name of the object, such as a person's full name, an email or TCP/IP address, its physical location such as country, locality, city and street address, and organisational attributes such as a department name or affiliation. Most countries have privacy laws regarding the publication of information about people.

The RFC also warns that turning an attribute value from its X.501 form into an LDAP string is not always reversible back to the same BER or DER form. The example is a distinguished name with one relative distinguished name holding one attribute type and value, where the type is commonName and the value is the text Sam. If that value came from the TeletexString choice the LDAP form is CN=Sam, and if it came from the PrintableString choice the LDAP form is also CN=Sam, even though the two original values were different. An application that needs to reconstruct the DER form of the value, such as one verifying an X.509 certificate, should not use the string representation of attribute syntaxes, but the hexadecimal form prefixed by the octothorpe instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Names often contain personal details, and privacy laws apply to publishing them. There is also a trap: the readable form of a name can lose which of several string types a value had, so anything that has to rebuild the original bytes should use the hexadecimal form instead.

The characters that have to be escaped in a value

items.title: Leading space or hash
items.text: A space or the hash character at the beginning of the value must be escaped.

items.title: Trailing space
items.text: A space at the end of the value must be escaped.

items.title: Special characters
items.text: A comma, plus sign, quotation mark, backslash, less-than, greater-than or semicolon must be escaped.

items.title: How to escape
items.text: Put a backslash before the character, or a backslash and two hexadecimal digits giving the byte for it.

viz.caption: The grammar of a distinguished name string, as given in the RFC

data.title: Distinguished name grammar
data.code:
distinguishedName = [name]
name       = name-component *("," name-component)
name-component = attributeTypeAndValue *("+" attributeTypeAndValue)
attributeTypeAndValue = attributeType "=" attributeValue
attributeType = (ALPHA 1*keychar) / oid
